proves: interface list and each interface's current mode/channel
notes: run first, on your own hardware

proves: the mode, channel, width and TX power the interface is actually using
notes: mode must be 'monitor' before capture

command: iw phy <phy> info | grep -A6 'Supported interface modes'
proves: whether the driver exposes monitor/AP modes — a hardware capability check, not a guess
whether a soft/hard block is silently preventing the radio from working
notes: common cause of 'monitor mode does nothing'

proves: which processes (NetworkManager/wpa_supplicant) will fight for the interface
notes: kill only in a lab VM; on a working machine prefer a dedicated adapter

command: ip link set <if> down && iw dev <if> set type monitor && ip link set <if> up
proves: the interface is now a passive observer
notes: revert with 'set type managed' when finished

proves: the channel the observer watches (one channel at a time)
notes: 5/6 GHz channels need the right regulatory domain

proves: the regulatory domain your radio obeys and the AP's advertised country
notes: read it; do not set a domain you are not entitled to use

proves: an inventory capture: BSSs, channels, security, clients, with per-AP context
notes: band-abg covers 2.4+5+6 GHz on capable hardware

command: tshark -r recon.pcapng -Y 'wlan.fc.type_subtype == 8' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.bssid -e wlan.ssid -e wlan.ds.current_channel -e wlan.rsn.akms.type
proves: the BSS inventory as fields you can cite (frame-numbered)
notes: subtype 8 = beacon

command: tshark -r recon.pcapng -Y 'wlan.fc.type_subtype == 4' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.sa -e wlan.ssid
proves: client intent: which SSIDs are being probed for (PNL leak)
notes: empty SSID = wildcard probe

proves: association behaviour: open (0), SAE (3), FT (2)
notes: auth algorithm alone does not prove the key exchange happened

proves: WPS-enabled BSSs and their WPS state from beacons
notes: verify against the WPS IE in the capture

command: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y 'wlan.tag.number == 48' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.rsn.akms.type -e wlan.rsn.pcs.type -e wlan.rsn.gcs.type -e wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpc -e wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpr
proves: the security policy as negotiated/announced (AKMs, ciphers, PMF bits)
notes: element 48 = RSN; prefer this over 'encryption = good' assumptions

command: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y 'wlan.tag.number == 221' -T fields -e frame.number -e wps.version -e wps.config_methods -e wps.ap_setup_locked
proves: WPS presence and state (version, methods, locked)
notes: vendor-specific element; WPS attributes are dissected by Wireshark

command: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y 'wlan.ssid contains "Corp"' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.bssid -e wlan.ssid
proves: which BSSIDs advertise a given SSID (ESS membership vs. look-alike)
notes: the SSID is a name; the BSSID is the radio

command: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y 'eapol.type == 3' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.sa -e wlan.da -e eapol.keydes.key_info -e eapol.keydes.replay_counter -e eapol.keydes.nonce
proves: the 4-way handshake messages and their roles (key_info bits), with nonces
notes: use key_info, not frame order, to classify M1–M4

proves: extracts crackable material (EAPOL MIC / PMKID) into hashcat 22000 format
notes: modern unified format; supersedes old separate modes

proves: which candidate passphrases have already been verified offline
notes: --show lists only recovered entries; absence of a line is the real result

proves: the audit rate and estimated time — the number that quantifies passphrase strength
notes: record rate + wall time as evidence

proves: whether the capture contains a PMKID value; its presence alone does not establish a clientless collection path or production exposure
notes: no output can mean the AP does not cache PMKs

proves: cracked MS-CHAPv2 material captured from an unvalidated PEAP client
notes: the material only exists if the client accepted a rogue authenticator

command: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y 'eap' -T fields -e frame.number -e eap.code -e eap.type -e eap.identity
proves: the EAP method, outer/inner identity, and exchange order
notes: type 1=Identity, 13=TLS, 25=PEAP, 21=TTLS, 26=MSCHAPv2

proves: the TLS handshake (ClientHello=1, Certificate=11, Alert=21) of the EAP tunnel
notes: an alert right after ClientHello = validation failure

command: tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y 'radius' -T fields -e frame.number -e radius.code -e radius.id -e radius.message_authenticator -e radius.tunnel_private_group_id
proves: RADIUS decisions, verifiable integrity and policy attributes
notes: attribute 81 = dynamic VLAN

proves: which identities were rejected, and how often (online guessing evidence)
notes: correlate with the AP/NAS and client logs

proves: what the supplicant does about the server certificate at connect time
notes: the -d/-dd log is client-side evidence for validation findings

proves: whether injection works against your own AP before any test relies on it
notes: capability check; never run against third-party infrastructure

proves: whether an unprotected deauth actually removes a specific client
notes: requires written authorisation; add PMF testing to the retest

proves: a rogue authenticator/BSS that presents a chosen SSID, security and certificate
notes: lab/authorised window only; stop conditions in the RoE

proves: what identity your rogue authenticator presents (parts of the validation test)
notes: compare with ca_cert/subject_match/domain_suffix_match in the client profile

proves: the integrity value that makes the capture an artefact
notes: store in the report next to every claim

proves: the reproducible extraction a reviewer can re-run
notes: the filter string belongs in the finding

proves: capture metadata: interface type, packet count, duration, timestamps
notes: use for provenance; if unavailable, note the tool used

command: tshark -r before.pcapng -Y '<same filter>' > before.txt; tshark -r after.pcapng -Y '<same filter>' > after.txt; diff before.txt after.txt
proves: the retest delta using an identical extraction
notes: the retest is evidence, not a promise

proves: device enumeration, authorized USB debugging state, and target hardware architecture
notes: check for unauthorized state; device prompt must be accepted

command: adb shell getprop ro.build.version.release && adb shell getprop ro.build.version.sdk
proves: Android OS release version and API level to evaluate OS security boundary changes
notes: API 24, 28, 31, 33, 34 introduce major platform breaking changes

proves: installs package with reinstall (-r) and grants all declared runtime permissions (-g)
notes: simplifies dynamic triage baseline setup on test devices

proves: forwards workstation TCP port to emulator/device socket for local proxying
notes: used for intercepting non-proxy-aware traffic or local test services

command: adb shell pm list packages -f | grep <pattern>
proves: locates base APK filesystem path in /data/app/ for pulling without root
notes: use adb pull to download the installed APK for static analysis

proves: prints binary AndroidManifest.xml without requiring full decompilation
notes: fastest way to inspect exported components and permissions in CI/CLI

proves: disassembles DEX bytecode to smali and decodes XML resources into human-readable files
notes: essential for modifying manifests, repacking, or auditing raw XML assets

proves: decompiles Dalvik bytecode directly into Java source files for static triage
notes: prefer jadx-gui for interactive cross-reference (XRef) call-site tracking

proves: verifies APK signature scheme compliance (v1, v2, v3, v4) and certificate fingerprints
notes: v1-only APKs are susceptible to Janus APK-DEX concatenation vulnerability

proves: prints signer certificate validity dates, subject DN, and public key algorithm
notes: audits whether debug keystores (CN=Android Debug) were accidentally released

proves: invokes exported Activity with an explicit intent carrying a custom deep-link URI
notes: tests whether Activity validates URI authority and path before loading sensitive data

command: adb shell am broadcast -a com.example.app.ACTION_SYNC -e token "test_val"
proves: sends an explicit or implicit broadcast intent with string extras to BroadcastReceivers
notes: unprotected receivers allow external apps to trigger internal state transitions

proves: starts a background Service across application boundaries
notes: exported services without signature permissions allow unauthorized operations

proves: queries exposed ContentProvider table data directly from terminal
notes: demonstrates missing android:permission or path-permission protections

proves: filters runtime system logs to target application tags and lifecycle events
notes: identifies sensitive credentials, tokens, or PII leaked to system logcat

proves: retrieves current Linux process ID assigned to the running application package
notes: required for attaching Frida, ltrace, or inspecting /proc/<pid>/ maps

proves: inspects private application sandbox files without needing a rooted device
notes: works only if android:debuggable=true is declared in the target build manifest

command: adb shell dumpsys package com.example.app | grep -A 10 "requested permissions:"
proves: dumps all permissions requested, granted, and revoked for the target package
notes: identifies whether dangerous permissions were granted by user or system

proves: enumerates all installed applications and active runtime PIDs on connected USB device
notes: verifies that frida-server is running on the device with matching architecture

proves: spawns target application and injects custom JavaScript hooks at early initialization
notes: use %resume in frida console to proceed after early hooks are placed

proves: attaches interactive mobile security assessment framework to target process
notes: provides high-level commands for memory search, clipboard, and hook automation

proves: runtime hook disabling TrustManager, OkHttp, and Network Security Config pinning
notes: hooking does not prove vulnerability; assess backend trust boundaries after bypass
